name: Jade Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary day at your accounting firm like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree in accounting, still learning the grant and tax rules while I prepare accounts and returns for nonprofit clients. I like calling a kitchen manager when the wages and timesheets do not match; I dislike the push to send a neat report before anyone can explain the difference. Rosa and I have grown children and about nine months of costs saved, so retirement is possible to discuss but not something I can assume.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our nonprofit clients still bring a folder of receipts, so a small software gain would leave most of my day familiar. I would still trace each wage figure back to the timesheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that a quicker return must still show the client what changed. The kitchen manager wants an answer when a grant line does not match the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI at work, and I prefer the ledger I can mark by hand. Our pay is above the usual junior rate and Rosa and I have nine months of expenses saved, so my own job feels steady here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep preparing assigned accounts and tax returns, using the paper timesheets to check payroll figures. I would bring the community kitchen’s mismatched grant line to my next review with senior accountant Dina so I can learn the rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our income in this mild picture. There are plenty of accounting firms nearby if an ordinary change ever forces a search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which client record needed a closer look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the kitchen had two volunteers listed as paid staff. The paper attendance sheet showed the difference between volunteers and paid staff. Dina checked my correction before I sent it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your household cushion mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa is my partner and works in social care, and our grown daughter pays her own rent. We have room for a bad month, though I would not confuse savings with a lifelong income.

say: I would show **client changes** beside a quicker return.
I would keep **paper timesheets** with each payroll figure.
think: I have **never used AI** on client accounts.
Nine months saved and **higher pay** make this mild change manageable.
do: Keep preparing **assigned nonprofit returns** and checking payroll against paper timesheets.
Take the **kitchen grant line** to Dina’s next paid review for a rule check.
feel: **Calm** about my work and income in the plateau.
S0.quote: The paper attendance sheet showed the difference between volunteers and paid staff.
fieldNote: Her **volunteer correction** shows the practical value of paper records, while Dina still reviews Jade’s junior tax decisions.
Higher pay, **nine months saved** and many nearby firms support a calm baseline without implying permanent retirement funding.

steps.text: Keep assigned nonprofit returns and check payroll against paper timesheets
Bring kitchen grant line to Dina’s paid review for rule check

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If software writes and checks most returns, even our charity clients may be told to send fewer questions to us. Junior checking is exactly the work that could be removed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the professional association to publish a clear rule for human sign off on automated charity accounts. I would tell clients to keep the original timesheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own paid hours could shrink even with nine months saved and a good wage today. Plenty of firms are nearby, but they may all be changing at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would join the association’s client-accountability meeting and ask our manager Dina to keep me on paid exception files while those files exist. If my hours actually fall, I would apply for posted nonprofit accounts roles elsewhere only with written pay covering our bills and a confirmed start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own week, though the cushion gives us time to look. I am not ready to put a charity’s payroll into an AI trial to prove I am flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the meeting I would ask who phones a kitchen worker whose pay was misread by software. A quicker payroll sheet will not explain a kitchen worker’s short wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can Dina guarantee those files?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dina can assign me the difficult files, but she cannot promise they will remain paid. I would keep only the hours the firm actually offers while I check posted roles.

say: I would seek **human sign off** rules through the association.
I would tell clients to keep **original timesheets**.
think: My **paid junior hours** could shrink as software takes checking.
Nine months saved and nearby firms buy time, not a **guaranteed role**.
do: Join the **association meeting** to ask who answers for automated payroll errors.
Keep **paid exception files** only while Dina assigns them.
If hours fall, seek **posted nonprofit accounts** with written bill covering pay and start.
feel: **Anxious** about a shorter paid week, with search time.
S1.quote: A quicker payroll sheet will not explain a kitchen worker’s short wages.
fieldNote: Jade turns her **association concern** into a concrete question about who explains a wrongly calculated kitchen worker wage.
She keeps **paid exception files** only while assigned and searches posted roles after actual reduced hours with written terms.

steps.text: Join association meeting to demand human payroll sign off
Keep paid exception files only while Dina assigns them
If hours fall, seek posted nonprofit job with written bill covering pay and start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 would handle the thinking in our tax desk before robots arrived around 2031. The kitchen itself might have more time for its hands-on work, but its accounts would not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm for written dates and tell the association to demand client appeal rights when an automated return is wrong. I would not promise any policy already exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my paid junior account work to end in the first year after AGI. Nine months saved helps us breathe, but my high wage pays a large share of our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep assigned paid returns only while they are offered and put the next two months of optional travel money into the reserve as new cash. After 2028 job loss, I would apply for posted paid grant-office roles only with written wages covering fixed bills and a confirmed start; I know grant paperwork faces AGI too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing a big part of our household income, even with savings. I can search deliberately, but I cannot make an employer create a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household plan changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Rosa and I had planned a long visit to our grown son this winter, and we can shorten it to a weekend. I would tell him why, without asking him to pay our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a grant role real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The grant office would need to advertise a real paid opening. I would not leave any remaining paid firm work for a friendly conversation about future vacancies.

say: I would demand **written paid-work dates** and client appeal rights.
I would say **grant paperwork** also faces AGI in 2028.
think: I expect my **junior wage** to end after 2028.
Nine months saved cannot replace the **large wage share** I bring home forever.
do: Shorten the **winter family visit** and put two months of freed travel money into reserves.
After job loss, seek **posted grant-office work** only with written bill covering wages and start; keep firm work only while paid.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected loss of a large household wage.
S2.quote: My partner Rosa and I had planned a long visit to our grown son this winter, and we can shorten it to a weekend.
fieldNote: The **shortened visit** creates new reserve cash from forgone travel spending, without assuming the grown son will fund her.
She knows **grant desks face AGI** too; an outside move depends on a posted paid opening and written household covering terms.

steps.text: Shorten winter visit with Rosa to a weekend
Put freed travel money from next two months into reserve
Keep assigned paid firm returns only while offered
After 2028 loss, seek posted grant job with written bill covering wage and start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years before 2031 lets me prepare for a different kind of client call, although the accounts desk still changes with AGI in 2031. The 2034 robots do not give the tax files another three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association for a paid route into explaining disputed grant decisions. I would not ask younger colleagues to do that work for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may be able to keep some paid client contact after 2031, but I do not know who will pay for it. Nine months saved lets me refuse an unpaid promise, not retire on an unknown number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Dina for a paid supervised place on two grant appeal calls with the firm’s specialist, Bea, and do the real calls if assigned. If the firm refuses, I will practise on free published appeal letters while keeping current paid returns only while offered, including the first year after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my wage but less rushed than in 2028. I can learn the appeal rules carefully if someone gives me paid time and a supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an appeal call involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An appeal call starts with the grant letter and the client’s bank record, not a script generated for me. I would need Bea to check my explanation before it goes into the file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid appeals dry up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid firm appeals dry up after 2031 and we still need my wage, I will apply for posted nonprofit liaison roles only with written pay covering bills and a confirmed start. I will not call a volunteer role a salary.

say: I would seek **paid grant-appeal learning**, not free client work.
I would set **2031** as the accounts deadline, before robots.
think: Paid client contact may survive, but I need a **real buyer** for it.
Nine months saved is not **retirement income** by itself.
do: Learn on **two appeal calls** only with Dina-assigned paid Bea-supervised time; otherwise practise free letters while offered paid returns last.
After 2031 paid appeals end, seek **posted liaison work** only if wages needed, with written bill covering pay and start.
feel: **Anxious** about paid work, with time to learn carefully.
S3.quote: An appeal call starts with the grant letter and the client’s bank record, not a script generated for me.
fieldNote: Two **real appeal calls** make retraining contingent on Dina assigning paid time and Bea supervising, with free letters as fallback.
A **liaison search** requires lost paid appeal work, continued wage need and posted written household fitting pay.

steps.text: Handle two appeals only if Dina assigns paid Bea-supervised calls
Otherwise practise free letters while paid returns remain offered after 2031
After 2031 appeals end, seek posted liaison only if wages needed; require written bill-covering pay/start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years brings me to 68 and may give Rosa and me a choice about work, but I cannot name that choice without our actual figures. AGI still reaches tax analysis in 2036, before 2039 robots matter to the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to count paid client appeals each year, not merely the number of new software licences. I would keep answering clients honestly while the firm pays me to do so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to stop working by then, or I might need the wage. Nine months saved today is a cushion, and grown children have their own lives; neither fact tells me our 2036 income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep assigned paid files and transfer eighty from each monthly wage into an emergency account if fixed bills allow, stopping if Rosa’s hours fall. After 2036, only if confirmed income still leaves a gap and the firm cuts my paid work, I would seek a posted charity finance role with written wages covering that gap, a start date and workable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy now because the long runway lets us measure the gap. If paid work stops before our bills are covered, I would be anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the monthly transfer work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The eighty is new cash from my wage, not the nine months already saved. I would check the standing order each winter against our actual heating bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you can afford to stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If we can stop, I would spend more time at the community kitchen without pretending it is paid employment. If we cannot, I will take only a real posted wage, not a volunteer title.

say: I would ask for **paid appeal counts** each year.
I would keep **honest client answers** while my work is paid.
think: I cannot decide whether to stop without **confirmed 2036 income**.
Nine months saved and grown children are no **guaranteed income**.
do: Keep **assigned paid files** while offered and transfer eighty monthly from wages if bills allow, pausing if Rosa loses hours.
After 2036 paid-work cuts, seek **posted charity finance** only if income falls short, with written gap-covering pay, start and workable hours.
feel: **Uneasy** now; anxious if wages stop before bills are met.
S4.quote: The eighty is new cash from my wage, not the nine months already saved.
fieldNote: Her **eighty monthly** is new wage saving, checked against heating costs and stopped if Rosa’s paid hours fall.
A **post-2036 role** depends on a verified income gap and actual paid-work cuts, not an assumed pension or child support.

steps.text: Keep assigned paid files only while firm offers them
Transfer eighty monthly from wages if bills allow; pause if Rosa’s hours fall
After 2036 cuts, seek posted charity job only if income gap; require written gap-covering pay/start/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my high junior wage could end quickly even with savings. Dated paid-work plans, client appeal rights and a real posted grant job with written wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would miss the kitchen calls. I would miss hearing the manager say a worker finally understands why the pay envelope changed.

headlineQuote: I would miss hearing the manager say a worker finally understands why the pay envelope changed.
portrait: Jade is a **58 year old junior** accountant with a bachelor’s degree who checks nonprofit payroll and tax returns under senior review.
She has **never used AI** and prefers paper timesheets and calls that let clients understand a corrected wage.
Her **higher pay**, Rosa’s social-care work, grown children, nine months saved and many nearby firms offer room without assured retirement income.
She asks the **professional association** for client rights and pursues paid supervised appeal learning before any conditional later job move.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could quickly remove her high junior wage despite the nine month cushion.
whatWouldHelp: **Dated paid-work plans**, client appeal rights and a posted grant job with written wages would help.
